title: The Stories Behind A Few Food Fads
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of several American food fads. They open with banter about TV dinners and Josh's childhood, then trace the Swanson TV dinner, which supposedly began with a surplus of Thanksgiving turkey and a train car kept moving to stay refrigerated, with salesman Jerry Thomas credited with the three-compartment tray. Next they cover post-World War II convenience foods, the history of gelatin and Jell-O (Peter Cooper, Charles Knox, May Wait, Francis Woodward, Jell-O shots), and the 1950s savory Jell-O mold craze with Ruth Clark's commentary. They then discuss the Crock-Pot and Mabel Hoffman's slow cooker cookbooks, and finish with the 1980s oat bran craze, its over-hyped studies, and the Harvard backlash. The episode ends with a listener mail segment about MS and a sign-off.

segments.title: Opening banter and TV dinner nostalgia
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Josh's hair and their childhood experiences with TV dinners, then set up the episode topic.

segments.title: History of the Swanson TV dinner
segments.summary: The story, which the hosts call possibly legend, says Swanson had surplus Thanksgiving turkey and shipped it on a refrigerated train; an employee contest and salesman Jerry Thomas's three-compartment tray led to the TV dinner, which was marketed around television and sold about ten million in its first full year.

segments.title: Post-war convenience food and gelatin history
segments.summary: After World War II, food companies sold off surplus wartime rations to consumers, and convenience foods took off. The history of gelatin is traced from its early use in France through Peter Cooper's powder and Charles Knox's dried sheets.

segments.title: Jell-O's origins and jello shots
segments.summary: May Wait is credited with naming Jell-O, and Francis Woodward bought the name for $450 and eventually made it succeed through traveling salesmen. The hosts discuss flavors, pudding, and the jello shot attributed to Tom Lehrer.

segments.title: 1950s savory Jell-O molds
segments.summary: The hosts describe the savory and novelty Jell-O mold craze of the 1950s and 60s, as Ruth Clark explained it, along with the companies' cookbooks and examples of odd molds.

segments.title: Crock-Pot and Mabel Hoffman's cookbooks
segments.summary: The Crock-Pot caught on because working mothers could cook all day. Mabel Hoffman's cookbook helped it take off by teaching how to make slow-cooked food taste better, and her later books followed.

segments.title: 1980s oat bran craze
segments.summary: Oat bran became a huge 1980s fad after cholesterol studies, Quaker Oats and Kellogg's marketing, and a Robert Kowalski book. A later Harvard study criticized it and the fad dropped off.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up and give contact information.
